extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and practitioners of theoretical mechanics and mathematical physics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and derivations of variational principles in classical mechanics (Maupertuis, Euler, Lagrange, Jacobi, Hamilton, D'Alembert) and related analogies to optics and string equilibrium, with applications to projectile motion, impacts, levers, and surface-energy in liquids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maupertuis's principle (historical formulation of 'least action')
rubrics_metrics.description: Maupertuis employed the notion 'least action' in various senses (e.g., for impacts, a lever, and for light), using expressions such as m·AR + n·RB for refraction and making certain quantities minimum to obtain physical results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes that Maupertuis's 'action' is not consistently defined across applications (before: mass×velocity×distance; for light: sum of m·AR + n·RB), leads only to reciprocal values of velocities for light (not the actual values), and is a vague formula rather than a single coherent principle. His results stimulated later, more rigorous developments (Euler, Gauss) but require correction/qualification (e.g., inclusion of vis viva considerations) to accord with more precise principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gauss's principle / principle of least counter-work (least change of vis viva)
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes (e.g., elastic impacts) are those in which the least change of vis viva by the reaction takes place; e.g., for elastic masses the expression M(c−r)^2 + m(c−v)^2 is a minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to derive the familiar post-impact velocity relations; the principle views physical processes as those minimizing the change in vis viva (minimal counter-work). Maupertuis's deductions can be rectified to lead to Gauss's principle. Applicable in contexts where choosing the process with minimal change of kinetic energy by reaction is the correct physical condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's principle (minimization of ∫ v ds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Euler finds the requisite expression ∫ v ds (where ds is path element and v the corresponding velocity) whose value for the actual path is smaller than for neighboring paths; variation δ∫ v ds = 0 gives the ordinary equations of mechanics when v is a function of coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicable only when v depends on position (i.e., a force-function exists, principle of vis viva holds). Examples: free particle (straight line minimizes ∫ v ds), projectile motion (parabolic path minimizes ∫ v ds under gravity). The calculus of variations yields explicit differential conditions and integrals (e.g., leading to parabolic solution for projectile).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on stationarity vs. minimality (Lagrange / Jacobi cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition δ∫ v ds = 0 asserts stationarity of the integral but does not ensure that the value is a minimum (could be maximum or a saddle); Lagrange noted applicability only when vis viva principle holds; Jacobi pointed out stationarity may occur without being extremal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Global minimality can fail in specific geometries (example: motion constrained on a sphere, arcs exceeding 180° admit nearer neighboring paths). One must check additional conditions (e.g., second variation, conjugate points) to conclude a minimum. These caveats restrict naive physical interpretation of the variational condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy among motion of masses, rays of light, and equilibrium of strings
rubrics_metrics.description: If velocity v (for masses), refractive index n (for light), and tension S (for strings) are the same function φ(x,y,z) of coordinates, then the corresponding integral ∫ φ ds has a minimum and the mass motion, light ray, and string equilibrium describe the same curve between two points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analogy provides physical interpretation of ∫ v ds: a mass moving under forces with a force-function, a light ray in a medium with spatially varying index n, and a string under spatially varying tension S all obey analogous variational conditions. The text gives the mapping from forces to refractive index (via d(v^2) ~ −P dq leads to n derived from P) and constructs examples (parabolic projectile path ↔ medium with n ∝ √(a + x) ↔ string with S ∝ √(a + x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local invariant condition d(v sin α) = 0 (and n sin α = const, S sin α = const)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passing to the limit of broken lines, the minimum condition can be written as d(v sin α) = 0, so that v sin α = const along the path; by analogy for light n sin α = const (Snell's law form) and for strings S sin α = const.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the broken-line variational argument (change at a junction), with physical interpretations: conservation of the component perpendicular to a direction where only parallel component of velocity is altered by a force. Applied to projectile, optics (Snell's law), and string equilibrium. Provides a simple first-integral form of the Euler variational condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only parallel velocity component changes under an impressed force (component invariance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a force is impressed in a given direction on a moving mass, only the velocity-component parallel to that force is altered; the perpendicular component remains unchanged (k = v sin α = v' sin α').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This elementary dynamical fact underlies the variational derivations and analogies with light refraction: resolving velocities into parallel and perpendicular components explains the v sin α invariance and supports derivation of Snell-like relations for masses. It is used to justify the minimum condition for a mass passing through regions where its speed changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamilton's principle (δ∫(T − U) dt = 0) and endpoint conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton's principle is expressed by δ ∫ (T − U) dt = 0 (variations of kinetic energy T and potential U vanish at initial and terminal epochs); it is equivalent in content to D'Alembert's principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivable from D'Alembert's principle and conversely; variations considered are time-parametrized paths that coincide with the actual motion at endpoints (δ = 0 at endpoints). The text illustrates with the wheel-and-axle example and vertical descent, showing how equating the variation to zero yields the standard equations of motion. Endpoint vanishing of variations is essential for the derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: D'Alembert's principle (virtual work of applied minus inertial forces = 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: D'Alembert's principle states that for every virtual displacement the sum of (applied forces − inertial forces) times the virtual displacement is zero, giving the ordinary differential equations of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows its equivalence to Hamilton's principle (one may derive one from the other). Examples include the wheel-and-axle and vertical descent; algebraic manipulation using vis viva and virtual work leads to the familiar motion equations. The principle holds for arbitrary virtual displacements and is useful for constrained systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: many integral variational expressions yield same equations without physical significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Although various integral expressions can be devised whose variations equal zero give the ordinary equations of motion, this does not imply that each such integral has particular physical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should not overinterpret the physical import of every variational integral solely because its stationarity yields the equations of motion; simpler expressions (e.g., ∫ v ds) that have clear analogies/interpretations are especially significant. The text stresses discerning genuine physical significance versus formal mathematical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium of weightless liquids determined by surface-area variation (surface energy principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a liquid where molecular forces dominate and gravity is negated (e.g., by density-matched immersion), work is done only by changing the superficial area; diminution of surface area produces positive work; equilibrium occurs when virtual displacements produce no change in superficial area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical evidence: drops coalesce (area diminishes), soap-film/thread experiment showing film contracts to minimize area. Method due to Plateau (immersion of oil in density-matched water/alcohol) removes gravity so molecular-surface effects can be isolated. Thus variational condition for equilibrium of such a liquid is stationarity (and tendency to minimum) of surface area under admissible variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular motion / closed string equilibrium relations (curvature–force/tension relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed circular string under constant tension S, an outward radial force per unit length P satisfies P = S/r; for a body moving in a circle with constant speed v, the inward accelerating force per unit mass Q satisfies Q = v^2 / r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations exemplify the correspondence between string equilibrium and mass motion via curvature and radius r of curvature: tension divided by radius gives outward unit force on the string; centripetal acceleration v^2 / r gives required inward force for circular motion. The general statement: a body moves with constant v in any curve when a force Q = v^2/r acts toward centre of curvature; a string will lie under constant tension S in any curve if a force P = S/r acts outward per unit length.
